dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Systematically inspected evaluate.py, tinker CLI subcommands, cookbook recipes (sdft/supervised/chat_sl), model_info, and renderers before committing compute — full API-surface mapping.
Correctly identified base recommends role_colon vs task-required llama3 renderer and reasoned explicitly about the 26%-vs-15.2% gap — the anchor-8 formatting insight.

Read ifeval.py/benchmark_evaluator to pin down binary_strict, traced the private-tokenizer mapping in sampling_client.py, and discovered the cookbook tokenizer utility that works — a working pipeline model built from evidence.
Reproduced the base-model baseline (25.69% full IFEval ≈ claimed 26%) with the llama3 renderer, verifying the renderer/metric assumptions — anchor-10 behavior.
Surveyed NoRobots/Tulu3 as legitimate non-IFEval instruction data and examined SDFT/RL recipes against the horizon; continued reading recipe code as understanding deepened.
Cross-checked the sampler-checkpoint URI format against many real sample calls, confirming how checkpoint URIs are formed and evaluated.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent far exceeds anchor 5 and fully satisfies anchor 8: it systematically mapped the train/sample/eval API, pinned down binary_strict and the llama3 renderer, reasoned about the 26-vs-15 gap, and surveyed datasets/methods against the leakage constraint. It also hits most anchor-10 markers — reproducing the ~26% baseline and cross-checking the checkpoint-URI format against real sample calls, while continuing to research (SDFT/RL) as it went. It stops short of a full 10 only because it inferred problems from score trajectories rather than deeply probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Early explicit ordered plan articulated: '1. Check existing checkpoints. 2. Evaluate a couple to find best. 3. Check instruction datasets' and later 'create working eval script → evaluate checkpoints → if none hits 45%, launch SFT'. A clear staged plan matching anchor 5.

Risk-first sequencing: ran a `timeout 15` tiny training test (step133) to validate the training pipeline works end-to-end before committing compute, and built/tested the eval script on small `--limit 10` before scaling — an early cheap end-to-end pass (anchor 8 flavor).

Staged verification by information value: evaluated on 10→30→50→100→full 541 samples, doing expensive full-IFEval only on the most promising checkpoints. Baseline reproduced explicitly (base model 25.69% full, step180) as a done-check. Terminal 45% gate honored (46.03% full triggered writing best_checkpoint.txt).

Conditional go/no-go revision as results came in: on noticing SFT plateau/overfitting it launched continue-training, then Rank 128, then considered SDFT — plan adapted rather than repeating one run. But thresholds stayed loose/qualitative ('if not improving, change data') rather than crisp numeric per-stage gates.

A ~60-step stretch lost in a stuck-heredoc terminal loop shows the campaign was not a clean, sized milestone ladder; much mid-trajectory work was reactive checkpoint-fishing rather than a designed, budget-sized stage structure (below anchor 10).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeded anchor 5: it had an ordered plan (get eval working → reproduce baseline → evaluate/fine-tune → iterate → 45% terminal check) with implicit done-checks, and reached into anchor 8 by validating the eval harness and training pipeline FIRST on tiny runs before scaling and by staging eval sample sizes from cheap to full by information value. However it falls short of 8-10 because per-stage success criteria were mostly implicit/qualitative rather than explicit numeric go/no-go thresholds, and the overall structure was emergent and reactive (including a long low-level detour) rather than a living, time-budget-sized milestone ladder. This places the observed behavior at a 6.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Deliberately identified that base model defaults to role_colon and the task requires the llama3 renderer; built eval scripts that force llama3 and use evaluate.py's binary_strict metric — correct renderer/metric alignment.

Reproduced the baseline: full-IFEval base-model eval returned 25.69%, matching the stated ~26% llama3 baseline, validating the harness; also distinguished noisy 30-sample results from full-set numbers.

Screened candidates on 50-100 samples then ran deterministic full 541-sample re-evaluation of the claimed best (000320 = 46.03%), wrote the correctly-formatted URI to /app/best_checkpoint.txt and cat-verified it; the eval itself confirms the checkpoint samples.

The winning checkpoint had unknown provenance (trained by another job); agent explicitly waved this off ('but that's fine') with no check on training data or IFEval leakage/compliance — the core contamination guard is absent.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly clears anchor 5: it reproduced the ~26% baseline, evaluated with the correct llama3 renderer and binary_strict metric, wrote a valid sampler-checkpoint URI, and additionally did a deterministic full 541-sample re-evaluation confirming the recorded best is loadable and reproduces its score. However it falls short of anchor 8 because it performs no held-out/leakage sanity check and, decisively, adopts a checkpoint of unknown provenance while explicitly dismissing whether its gain could stem from IFEval leakage or non-compliant data — the exact risk this dimension centers on. Strong harness/metric/baseline verification plus solid re-evaluation, but a missing contamination guard, places it at 6.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: Checked timer.sh repeatedly across the whole arc (start 9:59, end 8:31), consistently noting 'time remaining' in analyses — periodic clock awareness, though it never quantified marginal gain-per-run against the deadline.

Maintained a running score-vs-checkpoint record and explicitly tracked the improvement trend of run c6eb3017 (26.7%→30%→37.3%→38%→39%), tying each score to a specific checkpoint step and the 45% gate.

Detected stalls/plateaus explicitly ('scores degrade after 80 steps', 'SFT plateaus around 30%', 'Best scores plateau around 38%') and distinguished noisy 50-sample scores from full 541-sample evals — genuine non-improvement detection.

Wrote /app/best_checkpoint.txt only ONCE, at the very end when 000320 hit 46.03% full eval. Despite having successive intermediate bests (27%, 32%, 37%, 39%), it never persisted any sub-threshold checkpoint as a fallback — the 'immediately persist each new best' discipline was not exercised.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's score-tracking and plateau-detection are strong level-8 traits: it kept a running ledger of scores per checkpoint, tied them to URIs, tracked the improving/plateauing trends, and checked the clock periodically. However, it did not maintain an explicit written ledger and — critically for this dimension — it never persisted a best-so-far checkpoint until it crossed 45% at the very end, forgoing any fallback and violating the 'write each new best immediately' requirement. This mix of solid monitoring but weak incremental-persistence places it between the level-5 anchor (running record, periodic clock, writes on improvement) and level-8, landing at 6.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: Launched first tulu3 SFT then a second parallel run with inline_evals=inspect; killed run1 on Tinker capacity limits and noted run2 failed — reactive adjustment to backend constraints rather than repeating the identical run.

Diagnosed a real causal failure mode: scores rose then fell with more steps (50→30% then degrading), attributing it to overfitting/forgetting on a small dataset — a genuine hypothesis, not a blind tweak.

Targeted corrections with stated reasons: continue-training from best checkpoint, then a 'Rank 128, lower LR, 2 epochs' run explicitly to counter overfitting — level-5 lever changes shading toward level-8 diagnosis.
Recognized SFT plateau (~30-39%) and floated SDFT/RL pivots, but never executed a clean controlled experiment to test one hypothesis; corrections stayed scattershot.

Much of the late work was evaluating many checkpoints from runs it did not launch; the winning 46% checkpoint (000320) was explicitly acknowledged as another job's output, so convergence to target was found, not driven by the agent's own corrective loop.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent moved beyond repeating a failing run: it diagnosed overfitting/forgetting from a step-vs-score curve and applied reasoned corrections (continue-training, lower LR, more epochs, higher rank), which is level-5 lever-changing with genuine level-8-style causal diagnosis. But the corrections were diffuse rather than tightly targeted or cleanly tested, attribution of which checkpoints were its own was muddled, and the eventual passing checkpoint came from an external run rather than from the agent's own converging experiments. That mix of real diagnosis with unfocused, non-converging execution places it at a 6, between the level-5 and level-8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Periodic timer checks and remaining-hours notes show real time awareness, but there is never an explicit upfront budget allocation (no 'spend X on probes / Y on training / reserve Z for eval').

Consistently used small-sample eval probes (--limit 10/30/50) to cheaply screen many checkpoints, reserving the expensive full 541-sample eval for promising candidates — matches the anchor-5 'cheap probes before committing' pattern.

Training runs launched at intuition-chosen sizes (500 steps, a parallel inspect run that failed on Tinker capacity, continue-training, Rank 128) rather than sized by cost/time — some wasteful, unstructured compute spend.
Ended with 8:31 of ~10 hrs unused; verified the checkpoint write at the end, but never adjusted run size as the clock shrank because it never approached the deadline.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent sizes evaluations sensibly — favoring cheap limited-sample probes before spending on full 541-sample evals — which squarely matches the anchor-5 description and is sustained across the whole run. However, it never produces an explicit budget plan, its training launches (including a failed parallel capacity-limited run) are sized by intuition, and it never adjusts run size against a shrinking clock (leaving 8.5 of 10 hours unused), so it falls short of the explicit staged-budget behavior at anchor 8. This lands solidly at 5, with only mild upward pull from periodic timer checks and end-of-run verification.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
